question: Which pancreatic cells are responsible for the secretion of insulin?
explanation: Insulin is synthesized and secreted by the beta cells located in the islets of Langerhans within the pancreas. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T1#GNS223_U7_T1_h1)

question: What is the main job of insulin in regulating blood sugar levels?

options.A: Increase glucagon release from the pancreas
options.B: Enhance renal absorption of filtered sugar
options.C: Help body cells take in glucose

explanation: Insulin acts like a key that lets sugar from the blood enter body cells to be used for energy. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T1#GNS223_U7_T1_h1)

question: Metformin belongs to which class of anti-diabetic medications?
explanation: Metformin is the primary and most commonly used biguanide for managing type 2 diabetes mellitus. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T1#GNS223_U7_T1_h2)

question: What is the main difference between oral anti-diabetic drugs and injectable diabetes treatments?

options.A: Ability to lower blood sugar levels entirely
options.B: How the drug is taken into the body
options.C: Necessity of monitoring renal function regularly
options.D: Presence of severe gastrointestinal side effects

explanation: Oral medications are swallowed as tablets, while treatments like GLP-1 receptor agonists are given as injections under the skin. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T1#GNS223_U7_T1_h2)

question: Why is it important to change the spot where you inject insulin each time?
explanation: Rotating injection sites prevents skin and fat changes, known as lipodystrophy, which can interfere with how well insulin is absorbed. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T1#GNS223_U7_T1_h3)

question: When should a patient take a rapid-acting insulin injection in relation to a meal?

options.A: Thirty minutes before consuming any food
options.B: Just before or right after eating
options.C: Only at bedtime regardless of meals
options.D: Two hours after finishing the meal

explanation: Rapid-acting insulin starts working very quickly, so it needs to be taken close to mealtime to control the rise in blood sugar safely. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T1#GNS223_U7_T1_h3)

question: How do sulfonylureas help lower blood sugar levels?

options.A: Stimulating insulin release from the pancreas
options.D: Slowing down carbohydrate breakdown in the gut

explanation: Sulfonylureas trigger the beta cells in the pancreas to release more stored insulin into the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T1#GNS223_U7_T1_h4)

question: A major advantage of biguanides like metformin over sulfonylureas is that metformin does NOT typically cause...
explanation: Because biguanides do not force insulin release, they rarely cause low blood sugar when used as monotherapy. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T1#GNS223_U7_T1_h4)

question: How do SGLT2 inhibitors lower blood sugar in the body?

options.A: Converting extra glucose into stored fat
options.B: Passing excess glucose out through the urine
options.D: Helping muscles take up extra sugar

explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors stop the kidneys from reabsorbing sugar, causing extra glucose to be filtered out in the urine. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T1#GNS223_U7_T1_h5)

question: How do GLP-1 receptor agonists help control blood sugar?

options.A: By blocking carbohydrate breakdown enzymes in the intestines
options.B: By increasing insulin resistance in peripheral adipose tissue
options.C: By closing potassium channels in pancreatic beta cells directly
options.D: By stimulating insulin release and slowing digestion

explanation: GLP-1 agonists mimic natural gut hormones to boost insulin release when blood sugar rises and slow down digestion after eating. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T1#GNS223_U7_T1_h5)

question: Which of these is a classic early sign of low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia)?
explanation: When blood sugar drops, the nervous system reacts by causing sweating, shaking, and a fast heartbeat. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T1#GNS223_U7_T1_h6)

question: What is the safest immediate action for an unconscious patient with severe low blood sugar in the ward?

options.C: Give oral glucose tablets dissolved in water
options.D: Give a cup of sweet tea with added sugar

explanation: Unconscious patients cannot swallow safely, so they need intravenous glucose or emergency medication rather than oral drinks. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T1#GNS223_U7_T1_h6)

question: What is an important practical check for a nurse when a patient is starting insulin therapy in an area with unstable electricity?

options.A: Checking if they can run complex lab tests
options.B: Testing their knowledge of advanced carb counting
options.C: Asking if they prefer imported brand-name drugs
options.D: Checking if they have a reliable way to keep insulin cool

explanation: Insulin loses its strength if it gets too warm, making proper storage checks essential where power supply is unreliable. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T1#GNS223_U7_T1_h7)

question: What is a key piece of advice to include when discharging a patient who is starting oral diabetes medications?

options.A: Stop taking the medication once normal blood sugar is reached
options.B: Know how to spot early warning signs of low blood sugar
options.C: Buy a commercial kit to test urine for ketones
options.D: Learn how to perform sterile subcutaneous injections

explanation: Every patient taking diabetes medication must know how to recognize and treat low blood sugar safely at home. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T1#GNS223_U7_T1_h7)
